To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the severity of SBD in patients with atria fibrillation (AF) exhibits a significant variability over time and that this variability may be clinically relevant.

1) SDB is highly prevalent and associated with AF recurrence, 2) the AHI is highly variable over time, 3) SDB-severity is not adequately reflected by the AHI determined in only one overnight sleep study, and 4) nightly SDB-severities assessed by long-term sleep apnoea monitoring (LSAM) may be a better metric to determine SBD-severity in the context of AF.
nightly SDB-severities are not stable and that a single-night sleep study may not be sufficient to assess the true SDB-severity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new technologies for the assessment of SDB-severity over longer time periods and the evaluation of the impact of SDB on the occurrence of AF and the efficacy of AF-therapy.
the question, whether nightly SDB-severities are more important than single-night AHI values for the management of SDB and AF.
the question whether nightly SDB variability is a clinically relevant phenomenon in AF patients, which can be detected by long-term SDB monitoring.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SDB is associated with an increased risk of AF and that SDB treatment may reduce the recurrence of AF.
the nightly severity of SDB in individual AF patients is not stable but exhibits a considerable variability.

nightly sleep apnea severity assessment may better reflect the SDB-exposure in an individual patient, may be a more accurate metric to determine SBD-severity in the context of AF management and that it may help to improve the efficacy of SDB screening and management in patients with AF.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SDB-severities are not stable over time and that the use of long-term sleep monitoring may provide a more accurate assessment of SDB-severity than the single-night sleep study.
SDB-severe AF patients should be screened for SDB and treated with continuous positive air pressure (CPAP) therapy.
SDB is a dynamic process with considerable night-to-night fluctuations in severity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nightly SDB-severities are highly variable in AF patients and that this variability cannot be detected by one single-night sleep study.
nightly SDB-severities should be determined by a longitudinal assessment of nightly sleep studies rather than by a single-night assessment.
the current approach of using one overnight sleep study for SDB diagnosis in AF patients may underestimate the true SDB burden and the risk of AF in individual patients.
